findings.title: Cache deletion does not invalidate connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in UI
findings.body: The `deleteCacheMutation` only calls `onSuccess?.()` on success, unlike `disconnectMutation` which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `utils.viewer.apps.integrations` in its `onSettled`. If the parent component's `onChanged`/`onSuccess` prop doesn't itself trigger a refetch of the connectedCalendars query (it is optional and may be undefined), the dropdown will continue to show the old `cacheUpdatedAt` timestamp and cache-status UI after the cache has actually been deleted, giving the user incorrect information about cache state.

findings.title: Plain Error thrown instead of TRPCError with proper code
findings.body: When the credential isn't found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler throws a plain `Error("Credential not found or access denied")` instead of a `TRPCError` with a code like `NOT_FOUND` or `FORBIDDEN`. tRPC will surface this as an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), which is misleading for monitoring/alerting and prevents the client from distinguishing an authorization failure from an actual server error, unlike the convention typically used in sibling handlers.

findings.title: Directly instantiates CalendarCacheRepository, bypassing the CalendarCache factory/mock abstraction
findings.body: Elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. GoogleCalendarService) calendar cache access goes through `CalendarCache.init(...)`, which is the abstraction responsible for choosing between the real `CalendarCacheRepository` and the `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` (presumably gated by license/feature flag, given the mock exists specifically to disable calendar-cache behavior). Here, `new CalendarCacheRepository()` is instantiated directly, bypassing that selection logic. This means cache-status lookups run unconditionally regardless of whether the calendar-cache feature is actually enabled/licensed for the deployment, which is inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase gates this functionality.

findings.title: getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores cache expiry, showing stale timestamps as if cache is active
findings.body: `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups by `credentialId` and returns `_max(updatedAt)` without filtering on `expiresAt >= now()`. As a result, a credential whose cache rows have long expired will still report a 'last updated' timestamp, and the UI (CredentialActionsDropdown) will present it as current cache status. This misleads users into believing cached data is still being served when in fact the next read will be a cache miss and hit the live API.

findings.title: Cache timestamp is formatted with a hardcoded en-US locale
findings.body: The cache-updated timestamp is formatted using `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", {...})`, ignoring the user's actual locale/timezone preference used elsewhere in the app via `useLocale`/dayjs. For non-English locales this produces an inconsistent date format compared to the rest of the UI.

findings.title: dev:cron now relies on npx tsx without adding tsx as a dependency
findings.body: The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` (using the already-declared `ts-node` devDependency) to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not added to `devDependencies`. Using `npx` will attempt to fetch the package from the npm registry at invocation time (or use a globally cached version), which can produce version drift across environments and fails in network-restricted/offline CI or dev setups, unlike the project's convention of relying on locked workspace dependencies via yarn.

findings.title: updateManyByCredentialId incorrectly bumps updatedAt for all selected calendars of the credential, not just the ones actually refreshed
findings.body: `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` operates on the `selectedCalendars` parameter it is given (which can be a subset of all selected calendars for a credential, e.g. the `remainingCalendars` passed in from `unwatchCalendar`). After updating the cache only for that subset, it calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, which updates the `updatedAt` field for *every* SelectedCalendar row tied to that credential, including ones that were not part of the `selectedCalendars` argument and were not actually refreshed in this call. This causes `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` to misrepresent when a specific calendar's data was last cached, which is a data integrity issue even though the field isn't yet surfaced in the frontend (the PR author's own notes flag uncertainty about whether this update is needed at all).

findings.title: Ownership check excludes team/organization-owned credentials
findings.body: The authorization check `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })` only matches credentials with a direct `userId`. Team- or organization-managed Google Calendar credentials (where `userId` may be null and access is granted via team membership) will fail this check and the user will be unable to delete cache for those credentials even if they are legitimately authorized to manage them, despite the feature targeting calendar integrations broadly.

findings.title: No automated tests for the new deleteCache mutation, cache-status repository method, or UI dropdown
findings.body: This PR introduces a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), and a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`) that handles destructive actions (cache deletion, app disconnection) behind confirmation dialogs, but no unit, integration, or e2e tests were added for any of this logic. The PR's own review checklist acknowledges testing was manual-only and limited due to lack of a connected Google Calendar integration, leaving the deletion authorization logic, cache-status mapping, and dropdown rendering conditions unverified by CI.
